items.prompt: What kind of water do mangroves mainly grow in?

options.label: Fresh water only
options.feedback: Mangroves do not grow in pure fresh water; they live in coastal saline or brackish water, which contains salt.

options.label: Saline or brackish water
options.feedback: Correct. Mangroves grow mainly in coastal saline (salty) or brackish (slightly salty) water.

options.label: Distilled water
options.feedback: Distilled water has no salt, but mangroves are adapted to salty conditions, not pure water.

options.label: Underground freshwater springs
options.feedback: Mangroves grow along coasts and tidal rivers, not in underground freshwater springs.

items.ok_line: Mangroves thrive in salty or slightly salty coastal water.
items.ko_line: Remember, mangroves need salt in the water.
items.exp_text: Mangroves are shrubs or trees that grow mainly in coastal saline or brackish water. That means the water has salt, either fully salty like the sea or a mix of salt and fresh water. They are specially adapted to live where most plants cannot survive because of the salt.

items.prompt: Which part of the mangrove tree helps it breathe when its roots are underwater?

options.label: The leaves
options.feedback: Leaves handle gas exchange for photosynthesis, but they are not the breathing structures that help roots get oxygen in waterlogged mud.

options.label: The flowers
options.feedback: Flowers are for reproduction, not for absorbing oxygen for the roots.

options.label: The roots
options.feedback: Correct. Mangroves have special roots, like stilt roots and pneumatophores, that stick up above the water to absorb air.

options.label: The trunk
options.feedback: The trunk supports the tree, but it does not breathe for the submerged roots; that is the job of specialized roots.

items.ok_line: Mangrove roots stick up to get air.
items.ko_line: Think about which part rises above the mud.
items.exp_text: Mangroves live in waterlogged mud where there is little oxygen. To get air, they use specialized roots: the red mangrove props itself on stilt roots, and the black mangrove sends up pneumatophores, which are like straws sticking out of the soil. These roots absorb oxygen from the atmosphere.

items.prompt: What does the term 'mangal' refer to?

options.label: The entire mangrove forest or habitat
options.feedback: Correct. Mangal is another name for the whole mangrove biome, the salty woodland or shrubland habitat.

options.label: A single mangrove tree
options.feedback: A single tree is not called mangal; mangal refers to the whole forest community.

options.label: The root system of a mangrove
options.feedback: Roots are part of a tree, not the name for the entire habitat.

options.label: A type of fish that lives in mangroves
options.feedback: Mangal is not an animal; it is the name of the plant habitat.

items.ok_line: Mangal is the whole mangrove forest.
items.ko_line: Mangal names the habitat, not an individual plant.
items.exp_text: The word mangal is used for the mangrove biome, which is a distinct saline woodland or shrubland habitat. It covers the entire plant assemblage, not just one tree. Synonyms include mangrove forest biome and mangrove swamp.

items.prompt: Why do mangroves need to limit water loss from their leaves?

options.label: Because they have too much water in their roots
options.feedback: Mangroves have plenty of salty water, but the problem is the lack of fresh water, which is why they must conserve what they have.

options.label: Because fresh water is scarce in salty soils
options.feedback: Correct. In salty intertidal soils, fresh water is limited, so mangroves reduce the water they lose through their leaves.

options.label: Because their leaves are too small to hold water
options.feedback: Leaf size is not the reason; the scarcity of fresh water drives the need to limit loss.

options.label: Because they need to keep salt in their leaves
options.feedback: Limiting water loss is about conserving fresh water, not about retaining salt.

items.ok_line: Mangroves reduce water loss to keep fresh water.
items.ko_line: The issue is fresh water scarcity, not abundance.
items.exp_text: Mangroves live in salty soils where fresh water is scarce. To survive, they limit water loss through their leaves by closing their stomata and changing leaf orientation to avoid harsh sun. This helps them keep the little fresh water they can get.

options.label: Flat, wide leaves
options.feedback: Pneumatophores are not leaves; they are specialized roots that stick up from the soil.

options.label: Long, hanging vines
options.feedback: Vines are not roots; pneumatophores are upright, breathing structures.

options.label: Straws sticking up out of the soil
options.feedback: Correct. Pneumatophores are root-like structures that stick up like straws to breathe air.

options.label: Thick, woody trunks
options.feedback: Trunks are not pneumatophores; pneumatophores are much smaller, vertical roots.

items.ok_line: They look like straws in the mud.
items.ko_line: Pneumatophores are upright roots, not other plant parts.
items.exp_text: Pneumatophores are specialized root-like structures of the black mangrove. They stick up out of the soil like straws for breathing. They typically reach up to 30 cm tall, and in some species can grow over 3 meters.

items.prompt: How do red mangroves keep salt out of their system?

options.label: Roots that are impermeable and block salt
options.feedback: Correct. Red mangroves have highly suberised roots that act like a filter to exclude sodium salts.

options.label: By shedding all their leaves constantly
options.feedback: Shedding leaves is a different strategy, and red mangroves primarily exclude salt at the roots, not by shedding leaves.

options.label: By storing salt in their flowers
options.feedback: Flowers are not used for salt storage; roots handle salt exclusion.

options.label: By absorbing only fresh water from the air
options.feedback: Red mangroves take up salty water but filter it through their roots, not from air.

items.ko_line: The root filter is the main method for red mangroves.
items.exp_text: Red mangroves exclude salt using their roots, which are impermeable and impregnated with suberin. This acts as an ultrafiltration mechanism, stopping sodium salts from moving into the rest of the plant.

items.prompt: What happens to salt that builds up in a mangrove's shoot?

options.label: It is stored in the trunk forever
options.feedback: Salt is not stored in the trunk; it is concentrated in old leaves that the plant sheds.

options.label: It collects in old leaves that the plant drops
options.feedback: Correct. This is called the 'sacrificial leaf' strategy, where salt concentrates in old leaves that are then shed.

options.label: It is released through the roots
options.feedback: Salt exclusion happens at the roots, but any salt that gets into the shoot is handled by shedding leaves, not by releasing through roots.

options.label: It turns into sugar for the plant
options.feedback: Salt does not turn into sugar; it is removed by dropping leaves.

items.ok_line: Old leaves carry away the salt.
items.ko_line: The plant discards salt with old leaves.
items.exp_text: If salt accumulates in the shoot, it concentrates in old leaves, which the plant then sheds. This is known as the 'sacrificial leaf' strategy, helping the plant get rid of excess salt.

items.prompt: What is the salinity range that mangroves can tolerate?

options.label: Only pure fresh water
options.feedback: Mangroves cannot live in pure fresh water; they need some salt.

options.label: Only pure seawater at 3-4%
options.feedback: Mangroves can live in pure seawater, but that is not the only salinity they tolerate; they also handle brackish and saltier water.

options.label: Only water saltier than the ocean
options.feedback: They can handle saltier water, but they also survive in brackish water and normal seawater.

options.label: From brackish water up to twice the ocean's salinity
options.feedback: Correct. Mangroves tolerate salinity from brackish water to over twice the salinity of ocean seawater (up to 9%).

items.ok_line: Mangroves handle brackish to extra-salty water.
items.ko_line: The range is wide, not limited to one salinity.
items.exp_text: Mangroves can live in water with salinity ranging from brackish water, through pure seawater (3-4% salinity), up to water concentrated by evaporation to over twice the salinity of ocean seawater (up to 9% salinity).

options.label: A shrub or tree that grows mainly in coastal saline or brackish water
options.feedback: Correct. Mangroves are woody plants that live in salty or brackish coastal water.

options.label: A type of seaweed that floats in the open ocean
options.feedback: Incorrect. Seaweed is an alga, not a shrub or tree, and mangroves grow rooted in coastal shallows, not floating in open water.

options.label: A freshwater plant that lives only in deep lakes
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves need saline or brackish water; they do not grow in deep freshwater lakes.

options.label: A grass that grows in dry inland deserts
options.feedback: Incorrect. A mangrove is a woody shrub or tree, and it lives in wet coastal conditions, not dry deserts.

items.ok_line: A mangrove is a salt-tolerant shrub or tree of coastal waters.
items.ko_line: The other choices describe different kinds of plants or habitats.
items.exp_text: A mangrove is a shrub or tree that grows mainly in coastal saline or brackish water. It lives where most plants cannot survive, because it is specially adapted to salty, waterlogged conditions.

items.prompt: Where in the world do mangroves mainly grow?

options.label: Only in the coldest polar oceans
options.feedback: Incorrect. Polar seas are far too cold for mangroves, which need warm tropical and subtropical waters.

options.label: In tropical and subtropical coastal areas, mainly between latitudes 30° N and 30° S
options.feedback: Correct. Mangroves occur worldwide in these warm bands, with the largest area within 5° of the equator.

options.label: Inland on high mountain slopes
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves are coastal plants; they do not grow on mountains.

options.label: In deep ocean water far from any shore
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves need to root in coastal sediments, not float in the open sea.

items.ok_line: Mangroves grow in warm coastal regions near the equator.
items.ko_line: The correct habitat is tropical and subtropical coasts.
items.exp_text: Mangroves occur worldwide in tropical and subtropical coastal areas, mainly between latitudes 30° N and 30° S. Most of the world's mangroves lie within 5° of the equator, where the climate is warm and wet.
